title: Prospects for detecting the astrometric signature of Barnard’s Star b
authors: Tal-Or, L.; Zucker, S.; Ribas, I.; Anglada-Escudé, G.; Reiners, A.
read: Abstract, Table 1 and sections 2–4; saved author preprint, 5 pages. Table 1 is on PDF page 2.
summary: Models the detectability of a proposed 233-day planet’s tiny astrometric signal. Table 1 also preserves useful stellar proper motions: −802.8 ± 0.6 and +10362.5 ± 0.4 mas/year, in RA and declination respectively. These are Gaia-derived values quoted by the paper.
use: Use the stellar proper motion for an approximate displacement calculation. The planet calculation illustrates why angular scale and instrument precision matter.
limits: The proposed planet signal was subsequently challenged by R10. The 13.3 ± 1.3 microarcsec minimum signature is a conditional planetary prediction, not the star’s motion across a SPHEREx image. The publisher PDF returned HTTP 403; the corresponding public author preprint was saved instead.
equations: Equation 3, using the stellar proper motions, not a planetary wobble.

title: Exploring the dimming event of RW Aurigae A through multi-epoch VLT/X-shooter spectroscopy
authors: Koutoulaki, M.; Facchini, S.; Manara, C. F.; Natta, A.; Garcia Lopez, R.; Fedriani, R.; Caratti o Garatti, A.; Coffey, D.; Ray, T. P.
read: Sections 2, 3.1, 3.3, 4–6 and Figure 7; saved author preprint, 12 pages. Observing dates and flux factors are on PDF page 2; extinction discussion on pages 4–5.
summary: Compares a dim spectrum on 2015-03-19 with a bright spectrum on 2016-09-30. The bright-to-dim flux factors are 11.8 in B and up to 2.1 in K. Extinction and extra near-infrared dust emission jointly affect the comparison.
use: A strong source for wavelength-dependent variability and the distinction between observed dimming and a physical extinction interpretation.
limits: These are historical VLT observations of component A, not new SPHEREx observations or a forecast for the next dimming. Added thermal emission prevents a simple continuum ratio from uniquely measuring dust optical depth. Publisher PDF returned HTTP 403; matching author preprint saved.
equations: Equations 4 and 5; flux-ratio conversion and the restrictive assumptions of attenuation.

title: Precise Dynamical Masses of Epsilon Indi Ba and Bb: Evidence of Slowed Cooling at the L/T Transition
authors: Chen, M.; Li, Y.; Brandt, T. D.; Dupuy, T. J.; Cardoso, C. V.; McCaughrean, M. J.
venue: The Astronomical Journal; author preprint arXiv:2205.08077v1
read: Abstract, Table 3, sections 6.2–6.3, Table 4 and conclusions; saved 21-page preprint. Equation 17 is on PDF page 12; Table 4 on page 14.
summary: Uses resolved relative astrometry and absolute astrometry to infer masses of 66.92 ± 0.36 and 53.25 ± 0.29 Jupiter masses. Table 4 gives a period of 11.0197 ± 0.0076 years and angular semimajor axis of 661.58 ± 0.37 mas.
use: Confirms the challenge target is the Ba/Bb brown-dwarf pair. Supplies an explicit position–proper-motion–parallax model, a motion benchmark and an example of how dynamical masses are measured.
limits: The precise masses require resolved VLT measurements over many years. They cannot be recovered from a few blended SPHEREx frames. A mass–luminosity relation inferred for this coeval pair is not a universal law for every brown dwarf.
equations: Equations 2 and 3 for motion; Equation 13 for a contextual binary-mass consistency calculation.

title: Discovery of a ~250 K Brown Dwarf at 2 pc from the Sun
read: Sections 2–3, Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–2; saved 8-page preprint. Both numerical tables are on PDF page 5.
summary: Identifies a rapidly moving, very cold brown dwarf using WISE and Spitzer observations. Reports total proper motion 8.1 ± 0.1 arcsec/year and parallax 0.454 ± 0.045 arcsec. The paper explicitly separates the moving object from stationary blended sources.
use: A close match to the challenge’s moving-object use case. The saved evidence file transcribes four dated astrometric rows and distinguishes detections from upper limits.
limits: Historical measurements retain their original dates. The 225–260 K and 3–10 Jupiter-mass estimates depend on cooling models and an assumed age range. A WISE or Spitzer detection does not establish detectability in a narrower SPHEREx channel.
equations: Equation 3 and Figure 3; historical astrometry remains distinct from a new model fit.

title: Characteristics of the period changes in Mira-type variables
read: All 3 pages, with visual verification of Table 1 on printed page 129 / PDF page 2.
summary: The R Dra row gives pulsation period 246 days, O−C variation timescale 12500 ± 260 days, and O−C main-wave amplitude 11 ± 1. The final quantity is a timing amplitude, interpreted in days from the O−C context; the table itself omits unit headings.
use: Relevant target-specific numerical evidence within a comparative study. It supports a clear distinction between the short pulsation cycle and long-term changes in maximum timing.
limits: Not a paper devoted solely to R Dra. The long cycle is described as cyclic rather than strictly periodic. The 11-day timing amplitude is neither a magnitude amplitude nor a measured 11-day change in the pulsation period. No DOI has been verified.
equations: Equation 8 and Figure 5; no new period or O-C fit is claimed.

title: Mira Stars III: R Dra, R Gem, S Her, T Her, U Her and R Leo
authors: Isles, J. E.; Saw, D. R. B.
venue: Journal of the British Astronomical Association 99(4), 165–171
read: Scanned pages 165–167 visually inspected: dedicated R Dra discussion, Tables 1–2 and Figure 1a. Full 7-page scan saved.
summary: Provides an individual R Dra analysis within a six-star study. Table 1 gives a mean maximum-to-maximum interval of 245.32 days with SD 7.19 days over 96 intervals. Table 2 gives a combined mean period of 245.34 days and mean visual range 7.52–12.31 mag for the BAA series.
use: The strongest additional direct R Dra analysis located in this search; complements R05 with a light curve and explicit observational statistics.
limits: Historical visual photometry, not infrared. The SD describes cycle scatter, not a quoted uncertainty on a constant period. The approximately 54000 observations in the abstract cover all six stars, not R Dra alone. Still not a single-object-only paper; no DOI verified.
equations: Equation 8; cycle scatter is not an error of the mean.

title: SPHEREx Data Products
venue: SPHEREx Archive User Guide, live documentation snapshot
read: Spectral image HDUs, cutouts, spectral WCS and all-sky cube descriptions; HTML snapshot saved.
summary: Defines IMAGE (MJy/sr), FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI and PSF/EPSF products. Spectral-image pixels are 6.15 arcsec; the described all-sky cubes use 12.9-arcsec pixels. Wavelength response varies across each detector.
use: Controls units, pixel scale and wavelength matching in this report. It distinguishes visualization wavelength lookup tables from calibration products intended for science.
limits: Documentation evolves with releases. Record processing version and read the relevant headers. Six detector bands are not six independent complete 102-channel spectra. Do not substitute the all-sky cube pixel scale into calculations made for spectral images.
equations: Equations 6 and 7; surface-brightness units, solid angle and variance.

title: SPHEREx Cutout Capabilities
read: Access methods and the direct-URL cutout example; HTML snapshot saved.
summary: Documents cutouts of spectral-image multi-extension FITS files through the Data Explorer, direct URLs and Python tutorials.
use: Provides a practical path for obtaining small fields while preserving the image extensions and coordinate metadata.
limits: An example URL is not evidence that a specified target has suitable observations. Query the archive for real coverage and preserve the returned product identifiers.
equations: Input acquisition for Figure 6; no equation adopted.

title: SPHEREx Data Explorer Help on Spectra and Flags
read: Flag definitions and worked flag-inspection examples; HTML snapshot saved.
summary: Explains bit-encoded quality and processing flags, including SOURCE at bit 21 and FULLSAMPLE at bit 12. A set flag can convey processing or source information rather than automatically invalidate a pixel.
use: Justifies preserving flag names and using an explicit rejection policy instead of rejecting every nonzero flag value.
limits: A known-source flag can be relevant to contamination depending on context. This report does not prescribe a universal mask for every release or science case.
equations: Pixel eligibility for Equations 6 to 12 and the Figure 6 masking example.

title: Stellar Activity Manifesting at a One-year Alias Explains Barnard b as a False Positive
authors: Lubin, J.; Robertson, P.; Stefansson, G.; et al.
read: Abstract and discussion/conclusions on the 233-day signal; full 25-page preprint saved, not every derivation reviewed.
summary: New HPF observations and reanalysis favor a stellar-activity explanation for the earlier 233-day candidate signal.
use: Qualifies the historical assumption in R01. It prevents treating that candidate as an established motivation for a SPHEREx planet-wobble measurement.
limits: Addresses that specific candidate and data set; it is not a statement that Barnard’s Star has no planets. This review does not inventory the present-day planetary system.
equations: Interpretation boundary for Equation 3; no planet discovery claim.

title: Understanding the Lomb–Scargle Periodogram
venue: The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series; arXiv:1703.09824v1 (2017 preprint)
read: Conceptual least-squares formulation and sampling/alias discussions; full 55-page preprint saved. This is a targeted methods reading, not a replication.
summary: Explains periodic-signal searches with uneven sampling and why a periodogram peak needs interpretation in light of the sampling pattern and model.
use: Supports E11 and the decision to use all usable exposure times rather than infer a secure period from a few six-month snapshots.
limits: Lomb–Scargle does not prove astrophysical periodicity. A basic sinusoidal fit can be inadequate for a non-sinusoidal, changing Mira light curve.
equations: Equation 9, weighted floating-mean periodic modeling and alias limitations.

title: A Method for Optimal Image Subtraction
read: Abstract and section 2, particularly registration, reference-image choice and convolution-kernel fitting; full 8-page preprint saved.
summary: Develops image subtraction using a fitted convolution kernel and differential background after registration.
use: Supports the PSF-matching requirement and the schematic difference-image equation E8.
limits: This report does not reproduce the paper’s full kernel basis or establish its performance on SPHEREx. Detector response and spectral mismatch remain separate issues.
equations: Equations 10 and 11, explanatory subtraction and uncertainty models.

title: Accounting for Space Motion
read: SkyCoord.apply_space_motion examples and coordinate-epoch treatment; HTML snapshot saved.
summary: Shows how positions, distance, motion and reference time can be carried together when propagating coordinates to another epoch.
use: An implementation reference for E2 and for moving-target cross-matching.
limits: Propagating barycentric space motion is not by itself the full apparent-position calculation for a moving spacecraft observer. Parallax factors and the observation frame still matter.
equations: Equation 2, space-motion propagation versus observer-dependent apparent position.

title: Aperture Photometry
read: Aperture sums, background subtraction, errors and units sections; HTML snapshot saved.
summary: Describes measuring flux through apertures with masks, areas and uncertainties. Background subtraction and the physical units of the input require explicit attention.
use: Supports the measurement workflow behind E7; this report derives the MJy/sr-to-Jy conversion explicitly from units.
limits: Software output does not automatically correct blending, aperture losses, variable PSFs or all correlated errors. Pin a tested package version during implementation.
equations: Equations 6 and 7, aperture measurement and uncertainty assumptions.

title: SPHEREx Data Access
venue: SPHEREx Archive User Guide, live documentation snapshot
read: Browsable directories, SIA2/API access, Python access and spectral-image cutouts; HTML snapshot saved after a transient HTTP 503.
summary: Describes archive access through directories, interfaces, Python packages and the Data Explorer, including DR1 and QR3 spectral images.
use: A release-aware path for later obtaining the five targets’ real observations.
limits: An access route does not establish target coverage or detection. Keep failed requests and missing observations distinguishable from genuine nondetections.
equations: Archive discovery and provenance; no equation adopted.

title: SPHEREx Data Release 1 Overview
venue: Official release overview, accessed 2026-11-15 local time
read: Overview, dataset characteristics and citation instructions; complete short HTML page saved.
summary: States that DR1 was released in November 2026, includes reprocessed spectral images and a 102-channel all-sky cube, and that DR1 images are intended to be used with QR3 as a uniformly processed set.
use: Updates the report’s data plan. The image dataset DOI is 10.26131/IRSA678; the cube DOI is 10.26131/IRSA679.
limits: This report cites the documentation, not a measured result from those datasets. Future work using the actual products must also include the mission acknowledgement requested on this page.
equations: Dataset provenance for Figure 6; no equation adopted.

title: Water Maser Emission and the Visual Light Curve of R Draconis
authors: Osmer, S. J.; Benson, P. J.; Little-Marenin, I. R.
venue: Journal of the American Association of Variable Star Observers 20, 203-207
origin: Found through Google Scholar in Brave
read: All five scanned pages, including Figures 1 to 3, visually reviewed. ADS bibcode 1991JAVSO..20..203O.
summary: A study specifically of R Draconis. Monthly 22 GHz water-maser observations from November 1988 to July 1990 are compared with AAVSO visual photometry. The introduction gives a 245.5-day visual period. The source reports a phase relationship but is internally inconsistent about its numerical lag.
use: Direct object-specific evidence that different observing bands need separate timing and physical interpretation. Figure 2 contains a historical visual light curve.
limits: Abstract and section 2 say about 0.2 cycle, section 2 also says about 58 days, and the conclusion says 0.1 cycle. Do not silently select one as a precise validated lag. The record is sparse and the authors say there is only one strong maser peak. This is radio versus visual evidence, not a measured infrared phase lag. Scan text extraction does not recover the article; use the PDF.
equations: Supports the need to specify P and the zero point in Eq. 8 and keep wavelength-specific light curves. No maser lag is calculated or adopted.

title: SPHEREx Preliminary Mission Overview
authors: Alibay, F.; Sindiy, O. V.; Jansma, P. A. T.; Reynerson, C. M.; Rice, E. B.; Rocca, J.; Susca, S.; Unwin, S. C.; Akeson, R. L.; Mihaly, S. E.; Werner, M. S.
venue: 2023 IEEE Aerospace Conference, Big Sky, Montana, 4-11 March 2023
origin: IEEE Xplore SPHEREx search in Brave
read: Publisher title, authors, DOI, conference dates, visible abstract and introduction excerpt. Full PDF and remaining full text were not accessed; the page states that PDF access is unavailable.
summary: Pre-launch mission engineering overview. The visible abstract describes a planned all-sky spectral survey over 0.75 to 5.0 micrometres, four sky maps during a 25-month survey, and processing and archiving at IPAC.
use: Mission-design context in the introduction. Current release behavior is taken from IRSA documentation, not this pre-launch forecast.
limits: Abstract-level evidence only. No equations or protected figures were taken from inaccessible full text. The saved source record is a locally prepared metadata and reading note, not a downloaded IEEE article.
